t: Count Pairs Of Nodes — Degrees, Two Pointers, and Multi-Edge Corrections
o:
## Understanding the problem

We are given an undirected graph that may contain **parallel edges**, plus several threshold queries. For a pair of distinct nodes $(a, b)$, $\mathrm{incident}(a, b)$ counts every edge touching $a$ or $b$ — an edge joining $a$ to $b$ itself touches both endpoints but contributes only once to the pair. Each query $q$ asks: how many pairs $a < b$ satisfy $\mathrm{incident}(a, b) > q$?

**Example walkthrough** ($n = 4$, edges = [[1,2],[2,4],[1,3],[2,3],[2,1]], queries = [2,3]): node degrees are $\deg(1) = 3$, $\deg(2) = 4$, $\deg(3) = 2$, $\deg(4) = 1$, and nodes 1 and 2 are joined by two parallel edges. Pair values are $(1,2) = 5$, $(1,3) = 5$, $(1,4) = 4$, $(2,3) = 6$, $(2,4) = 5$, $(3,4) = 3$. Query 2 keeps all six pairs, giving 6; query 3 drops only $(3,4)$, giving 5.

The constraints ($n \le 2 \cdot 10^4$, $m \le 10^5$, at most 20 queries) forbid rescanning all $\approx 2 \cdot 10^8$ node pairs per query. The way out is the identity $\mathrm{incident}(a, b) = \deg(a) + \deg(b) - \mathrm{shared}(a, b)$: rank pairs by degree sums in bulk with a two-pointer sweep, then correct only the relatively few pairs that share an actual edge.
k: incident(a, b) = deg(a) + deg(b) − shared(a, b): the degree sum double-counts edges that run directly between the two nodes.
On a sorted array of degrees, a two-pointer sweep counts all pairs whose degree sum exceeds any threshold in linear time.
Only pairs joined by at least one edge feel the shared(a, b) correction — there are at most m distinct such pairs, so repairing them per query is cheap.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute force over all pairs
a.i: Precompute node degrees and a hash map counting parallel edges between each normalized pair (min, max). Each query then scans every pair a < b and evaluates the definition directly. This transcribes the statement literally and is a perfect correctness reference, but Θ(n²) work per query — roughly 4·10⁸ pair checks times 20 queries — is far beyond the limits.
s: Build deg[] for all nodes and a map shared keyed by (min, max) of each edge, storing multiplicities.
For each query q, initialize a counter to 0.
Iterate all pairs with 1 <= a < b <= n.
Increment the counter when deg[a] + deg[b] − shared[(a, b)] > q.
Append one counter value per query.
a.t: O(m + Q·n²) — every query rescans all Θ(n²) pairs; instructive but hopeless at n = 2·10^4
a.sp: O(n + m) — the degree array plus one map entry per distinct adjacent pair

a.n: Approach 2: Sorted degrees + two pointers with edge corrections (optimal)
a.i: Count in two layers. Layer one ignores shared(a, b): after sorting the degree array once, a two-pointer sweep counts pairs (i < j) with degree sum above q in O(n) per query, and every NON-adjacent pair is now answered exactly. Layer two repairs adjacency: among the at most m distinct adjacent pairs, one was over-counted exactly when its degree sum s exceeds q while its corrected value s − shared falls to at most q. Subtracting those yields exact answers, and the sorting cost amortizes across all queries.
s: Compute deg[] and a multiplicity map shared over normalized (min, max) pairs.
Sort a copy of the n degree values once.
Per query q: run the two-pointer sweep to get base = number of index pairs with degree sum > q.
For each distinct adjacent pair with degree sum s and multiplicity c, decrement base when s > q and s − c <= q.
Record the adjusted base as the answer.
a.t: O(n log n + m log m + Q·(n + m)) — sorting degrees and pair keys once, then linear sweeps per query
a.sp: O(n + m) — sorted degree copy plus the adjacent-pair map

w:
## Wrap-up

Mention the brute force in one breath to show you understand the definition, then pivot: the identity incident = deg(a) + deg(b) − shared lets a global degree-only count replace pair enumeration, with a cheap per-query correction over actual edges.

**Common pitfalls**

- Parallel edges: shared(a, b) can exceed 1 — the sample edge list contains [1,2] twice. A boolean adjacency set under-corrects.
- Normalize each pair as (min, max) so the correction loop sees the same keys the edges were stored under.
- The two-pointer count assumes two distinct positions i < j; never let a node pair with itself.
- Answers reach C(20000, 2) ≈ 2·10⁸; prefer 64-bit accumulators out of habit.

**Likely follow-ups:** support online edge insertions between queries (maintain degrees in a balanced BST or degree buckets), or return the qualifying pairs themselves instead of a count.
